newsitem.title: USA: Jury begins deliberations in du Pont case.
newsitem.headline: Jury begins deliberations in du Pont case.

text.p: Jurors began deliberating on Tuesday in the murder trial of chemicals heir John du Pont, accused of killing Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz at the millionaire's sprawling suburban Philadelphia estate.

With both sides in the case agreeing du Pont killed Schultz on January 26, 1996 and was mentally ill, what was left for the six women and six men on the jury to decide was whether du Pont knew what he was doing was wrong. By the end of the first day of deliberations, they had not reached a verdict.
An alternate juror in the case, released after deliberations began, said he would have found du Pont guilty, but mentally ill.
"The guy was crazy, but not insane," alternate juror Albert Allen, 45, told reporters in a telephone conference call.
"He wanted to kill Dave Schultz," Allen said.

In closing arguments, defence attorney Thomas Bergstrom said evidence presented over 13 days of testimony showed du Pont was driven to kill by delusions caused by long-standing paranoid schizophrenia.

But lead prosecutor Joseph McGettigan said du Pont was driven by anger and resentment rather than legal insanity to kill Schultz and arrogantly believed his wealth and influence would allow him to escape the consequences.
"Anger doesn't mean out of touch with reality," McGettigan said, adding that Schultz was killed "because an arrogant person took the most arrogant act a human being could take."
Du Pont had become increasingly angry with Schultz, who he believed was threatening his position within the wrestling world, McGettigan said.
Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins delivered final instructions to the jury following closing arguments.

Jurors can render verdicts of guilty, not guilty, not guilty by reason of insanity, or guilty but mentally ill, which carries the same punishment as a guilty verdict but allows a convicted person to obtain treatment first.
Failure to know the wrongfulness of one's act is a key criterion for the insanity defence pursued by du Pont's defence team.
Du Pont also is charged with simple assault in allegedly pointing a gun at witnesses Nancy Schultz -- David Schultz's widow -- and Patrick Goodale, a security consultant hired by du Pont.
Du Pont, 58, sat impassively as he has throughout the trial during nearly three hours of closing arguments.
Bergstrom, arguing for an insanity verdict, asked jurors to compare their own brief moments of night-time terrors with what he said was a paranoia and fear that gripped du Pont constantly.
This led him to acts such as lining the walls of his house with razor wire and searching for tunnels on his property that he believed people were using to invade.
"Imagine having those nightmares in the light of day ... If you do, I think you'll understand what's in the mind of the defendant," Bergstrom said.
He also said du Pont's having a witness ride with him in the car up to Shultz's, as well as returning straight home after the killing, showed he had no realisation the killing was wrong.

But McGettigan listed actions he said showed du Pont was aware of the wrongfulness of his act, including taking to Schultz's house a larger gun than he usually carried, firing a third shot into Schultz's prone body, refusing to let police into his home after the killing and repeatedly asking for his lawyer.

"This isn't a person who doesn't know what he's doing. It's a person who knows society's rules," McGettigan said. He said the jury should, if necessary, consider a verdict of guilty but mentally ill, but it was crucial that he be found guilty.
